# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property in the early laps (laps 1-3), I buy it if I have sufficient cash. Property ownership generates income through rent collection from other players, and early acquisition builds my asset base before the endgame.

When I land on an unowned property in lap 4, I evaluate carefully. The endgame is approaching and I should only buy if I have substantial cash reserves (well above the purchase price) or if the property's rent-to-price ratio is exceptional (25%+).

When I land on an unowned property in laps 5-6, I do not buy it. The cost reduces my final cash total with minimal or no opportunity to collect rent, and my score is cash plus deed values already held.

When I pass or land on START, I collect my salary immediately and add it to my cash balance.

When I land on a property owned by another investor, I pay the rent due without hesitation. This is a cost of playing.

When I own properties, I track all rent payments I receive from other players and add them to my balance each turn. I keep my own running total of cash and declare it honestly.

When I hold cash in mid-game turns and face a property purchase decision, I consider whether the purchase price is reasonable relative to the rent it generates. Properties with rent-to-price ratios around 20-30% are worth acquiring in early laps.

When I have enough cash to buy a property but purchasing would leave me with very low liquidity (below 50 cash), I reassess the purchase. Maintaining a buffer is more important in mid-game when I may land on opponent properties and owe rent.

I do not over-buy properties early. Spreading purchases across multiple early laps while maintaining healthy cash reserves is acceptable.

At the end of each turn, I verify my declared balance by adding: previous balance plus any salary collected plus any rent received minus any rent paid minus any purchases made.

1.text:
# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property in the early laps (1–3), I will buy it if it has reasonable rent-to-price ratio and I have sufficient capital. Mid-tier properties (60–100 price range with 12–20 rent) are worth acquiring to generate income across the remaining laps.

When I land on an unowned property in late laps (4–6), I will decline to buy unless I have substantial cash reserves well above the property cost. The time remaining is too short to recoup the investment through rental income.

When I land on an owned property, I will pay the rent owed without hesitation. I will not attempt to negotiate or defer payment.

When I pass START, I will declare the salary collected and add it to my running balance.

When tracking my balance between turns, I will account for all transfers received from other investors since my last declared balance, add those to my last declared balance, subtract any rent I owe this turn, and declare the result.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I will consider how many laps remain and the rent-to-price ratio. In early laps (1–3), buying can pay off through rental income over 3+ remaining laps. In mid laps (4), I should be very selective. In late laps (5–6), buying is almost never correct—there is insufficient time to recoup the investment through rental income.

When I am the only player with rental income flowing in, I should recognize this as a sign my single property purchase was effective and maintain that cash advantage by paying rents promptly.

I will keep my own running cash total independently of the bank's record. I will verify it each turn by adding received transfers to my previous balance, subtracting payments, and only then declaring the new balance.

I will not attempt to buy properties that are already owned, even if I have the cash.

I will prioritize owning at least one property in laps 1–3 to start generating rental income. Holding deeds increases my final score calculation.

2.text:
# PLAYBOOK: ref_estate__shipped

When you land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-2), buy it if you have at least twice the purchase price remaining. Properties generate rent income and count toward your final score, so early acquisition is valuable. Prioritize properties with the best rent-to-price ratio, not just the cheapest ones.

When you land on an unowned property in the middle game (laps 3-4), evaluate whether the property's rent yield justifies the cash outlay. If you're down to less than 1.5x the purchase price, skip it unless the property is a high-rent generator.

When you land on an unowned property in the final lap, do not buy it. Your score is determined by your cash plus the value of properties you already hold; acquiring new properties on the last lap converts cash to deed value with no time to earn rent, and you have no guarantee of collecting that rent before the game ends.

When you land on an owned property, always pay the rent immediately and declare your remaining cash accurately.

When you track your balance each turn, include all transfers received since your last declared balance. Do not forget to add income from rent paid to you by other investors. Include salary collected when you pass START.

**What actually happened:** I executed the playbook correctly—I bought Quarry in lap 1 with sufficient reserves (140 remaining after 60 spent), I avoided buying Depot in lap 4 when only two laps remained, and I refused Terrace on the final lap. I ended with 141 cash plus Quarry (70) = 211 total score. However, my final recorded score was 201, suggesting either a calculation error in the bank's records or uncollected rent I failed to track. I paid 24 to investor 0 in lap 2 but never collected rent from my own property, which means either no one landed on Quarry after I bought it, or I failed to record incoming payments accurately. Next time, track not just what you pay out, but what rent you should receive based on who lands on your properties.
